sections.title: The mission in plain language

blocks.text: NISAR stands for NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar. NASA and the Indian Space Research Organisation built one observatory with two active radar instruments. NASA supplied L SAR, with a wavelength near 24 cm. ISRO supplied S SAR, near 9.4 cm. Both use the same 12 m deployable reflector antenna. [1, 2, 3]

An active radar sends its own microwave pulses and measures the echoes returning from Earth. It can collect data at night and through ordinary cloud cover. The received signal still depends on moisture, surface structure, atmosphere, vegetation and viewing geometry; radar is not immune to environmental effects. [5]
What the mission actually measures

A focused radar image contains a complex signal: an amplitude and a phase for every valid pixel. Amplitude describes echo strength; squared amplitude gives power. Phase describes where the returning wave sits within a cycle. Comparing observations can reveal changes in scattering, changes in radar range, or movement of recognizable patterns. These are the measurement foundations of the scientific products. [5, 6, 7]
Your route through this guide

Start with the L-band scope, spacecraft and observation strategy. Then read the timeline and regional inventory, learn the radar quantities and products, and check quality before retrieving data. Portal instructions come before optional code examples. Numbered citations open the original references; figures link to their handbook pages.
A short vocabulary

An area of interest, or AOI, is the region you search or process. A granule is an archive product record and its associated assets. SAR means synthetic aperture radar. InSAR means comparing the phase of compatible radar observations. A dataset can mean an archive collection or an individual array inside a file; the context determines which.

blocks.text: How synthetic aperture radar makes a fine image

Pulse travel time determines slant range: range = speed of light × round trip delay / 2. While the spacecraft moves, the radar observes a target repeatedly. Coherent processing combines those echoes as though they came from a much longer antenna. This produces fine resolution along the flight path. Across the flight path, transmitted bandwidth helps determine range resolution. [5]
Why SweepSAR matters

SweepSAR transmits over a broad strip and follows returning echoes with a receive beam formed by array elements feeding the reflector. Scan on receive and coordinated pulse timing support an approximately 240 km swath with fine resolution. The result is repeated wide coverage and substantial data volume. The application receives ground processed archive files, not the spacecraft radio transmission. [4]

sections.title: Orbit, repeat visits and geographic coverage

blocks.text: The science orbit is approximately 747 km high with a 98.4° inclination. It is near polar, retrograde and sun synchronous. The orbital plane maintains approximately the same local solar time at equator crossings, near 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. Earth rotates below successive tracks; the spacecraft is continuously moving rather than hovering above a region. [1, 66]

NISAR looks to the left of its direction of travel. In a simplified northward ascending pass it observes toward the west; on a southward descending pass it observes toward the east. Sideways viewing also creates terrain foreshortening, layover and radar shadow. A map projection does not restore information missing in a shadow. [5]

The exact repeat cycle is 12 days for a consistent viewing geometry. Ascending and descending coverage can give roughly six day average sampling, but they are separate geometries. Interferometry needs compatible repeat observations. Acquisition mode and polarization follow a geographic and seasonal observation plan. [1, 9]
Where observations are planned

The near global L band domain covers land and ice approximately between 77.5° north and 87.5° south. The left looking orbit favors Antarctic coverage and leaves a northern polar gap. Ocean, land and ice observation modes differ; broad mission coverage does not mean every channel is collected everywhere. [9, 66]

S-band targets India and designated calibration and science sites, with a narrower observation domain than L-band. The reference observation plan describes modes and planned L-only/joint coverage; it is not a map of today’s downloadable or valid pixels. Inspect its original legend and compare with actual catalog footprints. [9, 70, 103]
Between observations

The handbook connects science goals to repeat observations, target masks and acquisition modes. A geographic footprint establishes where an observation may contribute; it does not observe the days between passes. A brief flood, sudden clearing or transient motion can occur between acquisitions. Show the actual dates and separate unobserved time from an observed absence of change. [53]

blocks.text: Acquisition time tells you when Earth was observed. Processing time tells you when a particular version was generated. Release time tells you when it became public. A fresh download can therefore contain an old observation or a newly reprocessed observation. The Composite Release ID (CRID) identifies the processing release. For example, the initial Provisional products used P05023. [10, 19]

Typical nominal latency is 2–10 hours for L0B and 36–72 hours for L1–L3. This is archive product latency rather than a promise of continuous coverage or immediate alerts. ASF plans validated reprocessing of earlier acquisitions in 2027. Check the live guide for the current inventory. [10]

blocks.text: What these numbers mean

A record is a catalog granule, not a unique date, an independent pixel, a full continent covered, or a usable change pair. Adjacent frames, both viewing directions and reprocessed records can contribute. Pair products represent intervals, so their counts are not directly comparable with single acquisition counts. The windows overlap and include neighboring land or ocean; do not sum the rows.

Zero GOFF records for the Africa window means none matched that collection and query, not that NISAR never observed Africa. Conversely, soil moisture records intersecting Antarctica do not establish valid soil retrieval on ice: footprints and collection membership are broader than a science valid pixel mask.
Records and bytes are different measures

The February BETA release exceeded 500 TB across more than 100 000 products [10]; that is a historical release total across product families. Current regional storage volumes require enumerating and deduplicating actual downloadable assets and summing their sizes. Multiplying these counts by a guessed file size would be misleading. A lightweight count query

import requests

params = {
    'short_name': 'NISAR_L2_GCOV_PROVISIONAL_V1',
    'bounding_box': '-25,34,45,72',
    'temporal': ('2026-06-17T00:00:00Z,'
                 '2026-10-15T00:00:00Z'),
    'page_size': 1
}
r = requests.get(
    'https://cmr.earthdata.nasa.gov/search/granules.json',
    params=params, timeout=60
)
r.raise_for_status()
print(int(r.headers['CMR-Hits']))

CMR-Hits reports all matching records while page_size=1 returns one example record. Substitute the documented collection short name for GUNW, GOFF or L3 SME2. Discovery is public; the metadata request does not download science arrays. Saved query URLs and responses accompany this guide. [25]

A useful inventory for a specific area also records acquisition dates, tracks, passes, modes, maturity, processing release, pixel overlap and file sizes. The number of compatible valid observations is a stronger measure of analysis readiness than a regional record count.

blocks.text: Power and decibels

For calibrated power P, dB = 10 log10(P). A two-date difference in dB equals 10 log10(Pafter/Pbefore), provided both observations use the same normalization and units. A change in displayed color is only meaningful with its quantity, units, dates and color range. The next chapter explains polarization and scattering; the motion chapter explains phase conversion. sections.title: Scattering, polarization and water

blocks.text: A radar pixel combines echoes from many objects. Their sizes, orientations, electrical properties and arrangement affect the return. Moisture can change the electrical response even when the land cover stays the same. A change in brightness is therefore evidence of changed scattering, not a unique explanation of what happened. [53]
Three common scattering situations

rows: Situation
Possible radar response
Interpretation limit
Smooth surface scattering
A smooth surface viewed obliquely can reflect energy away from the sensor and look dark.
Dark pixels can be open water, smooth dry ground or radar shadow. Wind and waves can brighten water.
Vegetation volume scattering
Branches and other differently oriented elements scatter and depolarize the signal.
Cross-polarized power can respond to vegetation structure, but moisture, incidence angle and noise also matter.
Double-bounce scattering
Energy can reflect between a relatively smooth surface and an upright trunk or structure.
Water beneath vegetation can increase the return. Brightness alone does not distinguish flooded vegetation from buildings or other geometry.

blocks.text: Read HH and HV as measurement channels

In the usual linear-polarization notation, the first letter denotes transmit polarization and the second receive polarization. HH is horizontal transmit / horizontal receive; HV is horizontal transmit / vertical receive. The channels sample different scattering behavior. Their usefulness depends on the acquisition mode, calibration and noise floor; a file need not contain every polarization. [53]

GCOV terms such as HHHH and HVHV represent co-channel powers from HH and HV complex signals. Other covariance terms can retain relationships between channels. HH/HV as a physical power ratio differs from subtracting arbitrary image values: a ratio becomes an HH-minus-HV difference when both powers are expressed consistently in dB. Never divide dB values to form a physical power ratio. [13, 53]

blocks.text: Why averaging helps but does not solve everything

Speckle is a consequence of coherent echoes and interference within a resolution cell. Averaging independent looks can stabilize estimates, at the cost of spatial detail. Neighboring or resampled pixels are not necessarily independent looks. Averaging can suppress a short event or blur a narrow river edge; spatial and temporal support must stay attached to the result. [53]

blocks.text: Posting is not resolution

Posting is output sample spacing. Resolution describes how close two features can be and still be separated. Multilooking or matching windows can make neighboring samples dependent. Resampling an 80 m science layer to a 10 m display grid does not create new 10 m scientific information.
Geocoding and terrain effects

Geocoded products place measurements on projected map grids, including UTM or polar projections as appropriate; they are not all latitude/longitude or all UTM. Geocoding alone does not remove radar shadow, layover, atmosphere, ionosphere or unwrapping errors. GCOV adds radiometric terrain correction, but its intensity remains sensitive to geometry and scattering. [11, 13, 15]

sections.title: From repeat passes to relative motion

blocks.text: A single image phase contains contributions from propagation distance and the arrangement of scatterers. An interferometric comparison becomes useful when two compatible observations retain enough common scattering behavior. The measured phase difference still includes geometry and environmental effects as well as possible ground motion. [53]

blocks.alt: Two radar observations of a ground point moving from A to A-prime, showing phase changes along the satellite line of sight.
blocks.caption: Figure 15-3, printed p. 155 / PDF p. 84. Cropped from the supplied NASA/JPL handbook. The drawing illustrates relative line-of-sight geometry; it is not an absolute vertical-height measurement. [53]

blocks.text: A phase cycle is a range-change scale

In the idealized two-way radar relation, the magnitude of LOS range change is wavelength × magnitude of the displacement-related phase change / (4π). At roughly 24 cm wavelength, π radians corresponds to about 6 cm and 2π to about 12 cm. Those are approximate physical scales, not accuracy estimates. The sign depends on phase ordering and product conventions; do not copy a sign from a teaching diagram without checking the delivered product. [53, 15]

Wrapped phase repeats every 2π. Unwrapping estimates which whole cycles connect neighboring samples; it can recover multiple cycles when the data support that inference. An integer-cycle error, a disconnected component or lost coherence can give an apparently smooth but incorrect result. Twelve centimeters is not a hard displacement ceiling. [53]
What the phase can contain

rows: Contribution
Meaning for a map
Useful check
Surface displacement
Motion projected along the radar line of sight.
Check acquisition order, pair interval and reference. One look direction does not independently resolve east, north and up.
Topography and orbit
Residual geometry and imperfect elevation/orbit information can affect phase.
Inspect geometry and correction information. A projected map grid does not remove every geometric error.
Neutral atmosphere
Water-vapor and pressure differences alter signal travel time.
Inspect supplied correction layers and regional spatial patterns; high coherence does not rule out a systematic atmospheric signal.
Ionosphere
Dispersive propagation effects are important for L-band.
Read correction availability, application settings and release notes. A supplied layer is not proof every error was removed.
Scattering changes and noise
Vegetation, water, snow, disturbance and instrument noise can reduce repeatability.
Check coherence, valid masks and connected components. Low coherence can have many causes.

blocks.text: A reference chooses a spatial zero

These phase tools report change relative to chosen ground, not an absolute Earth-fixed displacement. If the reference moves or contains a different residual atmospheric signal, the regional offset changes. Good shared coherence supports using the same cells; it does not prove that those cells were stable. The reference assistant checks support and consistency, while physical suitability still needs independent reasoning. [53]

A full year of observations from an annualized short record, or a direct vertical sinking rate.

sections.title: Uncertainty, calibration and validation

blocks.text: A clean-looking map is not the same as a reliable measurement. The handbook separates instrument calibration, measurement error and independent validation. Its performance requirements describe mission design objectives under specified conditions, not a promise that every pixel or this app meets that accuracy. [53]
Calibration and validation answer different questions

rows: Term
Question answered
Examples of evidence
Calibration
How are instrument responses related to physical measurements, and are channels/geolocation stable?
Known reflectors, radiometric reference targets, channel calibration and instrument characterization.
Validation
How close is a derived quantity to an independent reference for this place, time and scale?
GNSS for displacement, field wetness measurements, suitable independent imagery or forest inventories.
Software verification
Does the implementation reproduce specified calculations and known test cases?
Synthetic known-value tests, saved-recipe replay and provenance checks. This alone does not establish environmental accuracy.

blocks.text: Coverage and uncertainty are not the same

A catalog footprint means the file intersects a region, not that every pixel contains a usable measurement. Valid coverage can shrink after masks, thresholds, common-date support and a reference requirement are applied. A missing result is unknown rather than zero change. Common support makes a temporal comparison fairer but can exclude a large part of the selected region. [53]
Thresholds, sensitivity and display ranges

A threshold sensitivity map asks how a result changes when a chosen setting changes. It is not automatically a confidence interval. A coherence threshold is a screening choice, not a universal accuracy certificate. The 2nd–98th percentile color range is a visualization stretch, not 96% confidence in the measurement. Palette and opacity changes do not improve or alter the exported numeric values.
A practical reading sequence

rows: Step
Question
1 · Measurement
What quantity and unit does this layer show, and at which date or pair interval?
2 · Support
How much of the region has accepted data, and is the comparison footprint the same through time?
3 · Assumptions
Which geometry, thresholds, correction settings, model and reference define this result?
4 · Independent evidence
What separate observation can confirm the interpretation at a compatible date and spatial scale?
5 · Honest conclusion
What was measured, what is only a candidate explanation, and what remains unobserved?

blocks.text: The handbook describes validation using independent geodetic, ecological, optical and field observations. The exact evidence depends on the quantity: an optical forest boundary can test a candidate patch’s spatial agreement, while a LOS displacement needs a compatible displacement reference. Agreement in color between two maps is not a quantitative accuracy assessment. [53]

Prepare your account

Use your own Earthdata Login in this app’s Connection tab. The app keeps the active login in server memory; do not put a password in source code or shared notebooks. Verify the account email and accept the required data-access agreements when requested. Discovery is generally public; reading science files requires authorization. blocks.text: These examples are for external scripts, not actions performed by this page. Their fixed dates and small result limits are teaching choices, not a recommended scientific sequence. Inspect results, select compatible observations, and review current collection/version and client documentation before enabling a transfer.
1 · Find metadata with asf_search

asf_search is the ASF Python SAR client. The following metadata query follows the official NISAR filters. It does not download science arrays. Install the library in a supported environment, then pin the version that your team verifies. [23, 57]

from pathlib import Path
import json
import asf_search as asf

results = asf.search(
    dataset='NISAR', processingLevel='GCOV',
    dataMaturity='PROVISIONAL',
    intersectsWith=(
        'POLYGON((-99.3 19.2,-98.9 19.2,-98.9 19.7,'
        '-99.3 19.7,-99.3 19.2))'
    ),
    start='2026-06-17T00:00:00Z',
    end='2026-10-15T00:00:00Z', maxResults=20
)
Path('discovery.geojson').write_text(
    json.dumps(results.geojson(), indent=2), encoding='utf-8'
)
for item in results:
    print(item.properties['fileID'])
Select scientifically compatible observations

WKT polygon coordinates are longitude then latitude. This rectangle is an example near Mexico City, not a selected application location. Group results by track, pass, frame, subband, channel and bandwidth, then check maturity and CRID. The first two search hits may be incompatible. maxResults caps a response; it does not count the full inventory. [23]
For a longer inventory, use the documented paging or generator workflow. Keep filters, query time and original identifiers. A successful metadata request does not test authorized science access. [23]
2 · Retrieve reviewed HDF5 assets

The search result can contain science and QA assets. Select the intended product first, then filter the science HDF5 URLs. This continuation keeps download selection separate from discovery and privately prompts for your existing credentials. [56, 65]

from getpass import getpass
from pathlib import Path
import asf_search as asf

# Continue with reviewed results from the preceding example.
selected = asf.ASFSearchResults(results[:1])
urls = selected.find_urls(
    extension='.h5', pattern=r'^(?!.*QA_STATS).*',
    directAccess=False
)
print(urls)  # inspect the intended science assets

session = asf.ASFSession().auth_with_creds(
    input('Earthdata username: '),
    getpass('Earthdata password: ')
)
raw = Path('data/raw')
raw.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
# Enable after checking the chosen product and available space:
# asf.download_urls(urls, path=str(raw), session=session,
#                   processes=1)

results[:1] is a small transfer example. Replace it with an explicitly reviewed selection for a real sequence. Verify the downloaded file opens as HDF5 and contains the expected datasets. Preserve metadata, checksums where available and the product ID; a saved login error page is not a science file.
Other supported authentication mechanisms

A correctly protected .netrc file avoids repeated prompts; its Earthdata entry uses machine urs.earthdata.nasa.gov, login and password. Restrict access to the file owner. ASF also supports tokens and reusable cookie authentication. Keep these out of shared notebooks and source control. An Earthdata token is different from an AWS session credential. [65]
3 · Use ASF’s HTTP SearchAPI

SearchAPI is an HTTP discovery service. It returns metadata and asset links, while a second authenticated operation retrieves science bytes. Use it when you prefer a language independent catalog interface. Python asf_search is an alternative client, not a required wrapper around this endpoint. [63, 64]

import requests

endpoint = (
    'https://api.daac.asf.alaska.edu/services/search/param'
)
params = {
    'dataset': 'NISAR', 'processingLevel': 'GCOV',
    'dataMaturity': 'PROVISIONAL',
    'bbox': '-99.3,19.2,-98.9,19.7',
    'start': '2026-06-17T00:00:00Z',
    'end': '2026-10-15T00:00:00Z',
    'maxResults': 2, 'output': 'geojson'
}
r = requests.get(endpoint, params=params, timeout=60)
r.raise_for_status()
catalog = r.json()
print(len(catalog['features']))

The saved discovery receipt from 15 October 2026 lists two PROVISIONAL results from different tracks and pass directions. Use it to check catalog discovery. Change analysis requires compatible observations and verified science files.
Coordinate and output rules

bbox is west, south, east, north. Parameter names are case sensitive; times are UTC. GeoJSON provides geometry and properties. CSV and other outputs support alternative inspection workflows. Choosing an output format does not convert the HDF5 science arrays into that format. [64]
4 · Use earthaccess and NASA CMR

earthaccess is a NASA wide Python client for login, catalog search, download and supported remote opening. It is useful when the same system will access several NASA datasets. Select a documented NISAR collection rather than assuming a generic ASF collection name. [24]

import earthaccess

earthaccess.login()
items = earthaccess.search_data(
    short_name='NISAR_L2_GCOV_PROVISIONAL_V1',
    bounding_box=(-99.3, 19.2, -98.9, 19.7),
    temporal=('2026-06-17', '2026-10-15'), count=20
)
# Inspect and select compatible granules before enabling transfer.
# paths = earthaccess.download(items[:1], 'data/raw')
CMR is the underlying NASA catalog

The Common Metadata Repository, CMR, exposes collections and granules through REST endpoints. Resolve the exact product, maturity and collection version; query its granules; then inspect science, browse and metadata links separately. Collection concept IDs can change. The regional inventory uses this public service and its CMR-Hits count header. [25]

ASF clients and earthaccess can depend on the same NASA catalog infrastructure. Changing the client does not guarantee an independent fallback during a CMR outage. The regional inventory chapter includes a separate minimal CMR count query. [20, 24, 25]

sections.title: Reading the science handbook today

blocks.text: The supplied NASA-ISRO SAR Mission Science Users’ Handbook has an August 2019 Version 1 cover and a prelaunch mission description. Its front matter also gives a 2018 suggested citation. It is valuable for radar physics and the reasoning behind mission measurements; dates, planned performance, product delivery and archive statements need current confirmation. NASA now identifies a second edition as its updated user guide. [53, 70]
Keep the physics; check the operational details

rows: Topic
What the supplied edition says
How to read it in this app
Launch
January 2022 was the planned launch.
Actual launch: 30 July 2025. Launch is the broad search start, not proof that a science product exists for that date. [103]
Radar wavelengths
Early summaries describe S-band as 12 cm; the L-band value is about 24 cm.
Current NASA mission values: about 24 cm for L-band and 9.4 cm for S-band. All four app input products use L-band. [103]
Coverage and timing
A repeating observation strategy and planned target masks.
Use the actual acquisition dates, footprints, valid samples and matching track/frame. A 12-day repeat does not guarantee a usable observation every 12 days.
Product hierarchy
Mission-level science goals, proposed algorithms and planned Level 3 outputs.
The implemented inputs remain GCOV, GUNW, GOFF and SME2. A proposed biomass, inundation or ice product is not an additional delivered app input. [11]
Performance and delivery
Design requirements, projected precision and planned release/response schedules.
These are not accuracy certificates or delivery guarantees for your selected files or this app. Read each release’s current quality notes. [10]

sections.title: How to interpret the evidence and reported metrics
sections.body:
Evidence category | What it establishes | What it does not establish
Actual NISAR research | A method was applied to mission observations or products. | Uniform global accuracy or suitability for every product release.
Agency demonstration | A credible mission example and useful measurement context. | A complete validation protocol, error budget or reproducible processing package.
Earlier satellite or airborne experiment | Empirical performance under the stated sensor and site conditions. | The same result under NISAR geometry, cadence, calibration and noise.
Simulation or prelaunch method | Algorithm feasibility or sensitivity under modeled assumptions. | On orbit end to end product validation.
Processing method or synthesis | Reusable methods, scientific requirements or error concepts. | A new calibrated physical observation on its own.
Metadata only lead | A publication exists and is potentially relevant. | Its detailed experimental outcome has been independently checked here.
Metrics are not interchangeable
Overall accuracy counts correct classifications across the evaluated samples. User accuracy describes reliability of a mapped class; producer accuracy describes how much of the reference class was detected. F1 balances precision and recall. Correlation measures association rather than absolute error. RMSE includes bias; unbiased RMSE removes mean bias. Dynamic range in dB is not an accuracy percentage.
Algorithm agreement is not ground truth accuracy. A modeled fault or dike parameter is not a directly measured pixel. A velocity baseline is different from a temporal velocity change. Every number below retains its own study context; no cross study league table is calculated.
Terms used in the annotations
RMSE means root mean square error; ubRMSE is its unbiased form. GNSS ground stations measure positions using navigation satellites. A DEM is a digital elevation model. SWE is snow water equivalent, the depth of water represented by the snow. GPR means ground penetrating radar. UAVSAR is an airborne L band radar, not the NISAR satellite. In situ means measured at the site. SNOTEL is a network of snow and weather monitoring stations.

blocks.text: Actual NISAR observations of subsidence, earthquakes, volcanic activity and Antarctic scattering. Read each source’s evidence level and limitations.
R01  JPL 29 April 2026 — NISAR maps extreme subsidence in Mexico City
Ground deformation  •  Agency demonstration
Data and setting: Actual NISAR L band; Mexico City, 25 October 2025–17 January 2026.
Technique: Repeated radar displacement mapping.
Reported finding: Some areas subsided by a few centimeters per month.
Limits: Agency presentation rather than a validation paper; no error budget is reported.
Review depth: Agency article.
https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/us-indian-space-mission-maps-extreme-subsidence-in-mexico-city/
R02  NASA Earth Observatory 10 July 2026 — Where Venezuela earthquakes shifted the ground
Ground deformation  •  Agency demonstration
Data and setting: Actual NISAR observations before and after the June 2026 Venezuela earthquakes.
Technique: Compare radar range change across compatible pre and post event observations.
Reported finding: NASA shows the spatial pattern of ground shifts associated with the earthquakes.
Limits: Line of sight combines motion components; this is not a direct building damage assessment.
Review depth: Agency article.
https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/where-venezuelas-earthquakes-shifted-the-ground/
R03  JPL 24 September 2026 — NISAR time lapse of the Krasheninnikov eruption
Volcanic surface change  •  Agency demonstration
Data and setting: Actual NISAR; 17 frames from December 2025 to mid August 2026, Krasheninnikov.
Technique: Time lapse radar backscatter inspection.
Reported finding: Changing bright rough surfaces reveal the evolving lava field.
Limits: Radar brightness is not a direct temperature or lava volume measurement; no classification accuracy supplied.
Review depth: Agency article.
https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/us-india-satellite-captures-time-lapse-video-of-volcanic-eruption/
R04  JPL 21 July 2026 — NISAR data release and Antarctic polarimetric imagery
Polar surface structure  •  Agency demonstration
Data and setting: Actual NISAR; East Antarctic nunatak imagery from August 2025.
Technique: Polarimetric imaging of rock and ice scattering.
Reported finding: Contrasting radar responses distinguish surface structures.
Limits: A single polarimetric view is structural context, not a temporal change or ice velocity validation.
Review depth: Agency article.
https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/us-india-satellite-delivers-data-reveals-hummingbird-in-antarctica/
R18  Xu et al. (2026) — NISAR observations of contracting dike-driven crustal deformation during the 2025 Hayli Gubbi Eruption, Afar
Volcanic deformation  •  Peer reviewed; actual NISAR
Data and setting: NISAR L1 RSLC, Sentinel 1 ascending and descending interferometry, optical imagery and a DEM.
Technique: Combine radar viewing geometries and fit tensile dislocation models.
Reported finding: NISAR line of sight deformation reached about 0.7 m near a northern caldera; the analysis favors two contracting dikes beneath Erta Ale.

Limits: The three dimensional interpretation combines multiple viewing geometries and modeling assumptions. A single NISAR view does not independently measure all motion components. Online corrected proof dated June 2026.
Review depth: Publisher abstract and results extracts; associated author dataset identified.

R07  Watanabe et al 2021 — Refined algorithm for forest early warning system with ALOS 2 PALSAR 2 ScanSAR data in tropical forest regions. Remote Sensing of Environment 265 112643
Forest disturbance  •  Peer reviewed; earlier satellite
Data and setting: ALOS 2 PALSAR 2 ScanSAR tropical forest sites.
Technique: Refined change detection using HH, HV and their ratios.
Reported finding: Across 11 sites: user accuracy 85%, producer accuracy 63.8%; a broader 191 site evaluation reported user accuracy 71.1%.
Limits: User and producer accuracy measure different errors; do not merge evaluations with different samples.
Review depth: Publisher abstract.

R08  Balling Slagter van der Woude Herold and Reiche 2024 — ALOS 2 PALSAR 2 ScanSAR and Sentinel 1 data for timely tropical forest disturbance mapping in Sumatra. International Journal of Applied Earth Observation 132 103994
Forest disturbance  •  Peer reviewed; earlier satellites
Data and setting: ALOS 2 L band and Sentinel 1 C band, Sumatra.
Technique: Combine complementary time series for disturbance alerts.
Reported finding: Producer accuracy 78.9 ± 11.9% for fusion versus 40.8 ± 6.3% for L alone and 63.3 ± 9.6% for C alone.
Limits: Values belong to the study sampling and alert protocol; they are not NISAR performance specifications.
Review depth: Publisher abstract.

Post fire vegetation  •  Peer reviewed; earlier SAR
Data and setting: Multi frequency radar over Mediterranean and boreal forest regrowth chronosequences.
Technique: Relate radar response to time since fire and vegetation recovery.
Reported finding: Approximate response dynamic range: L 8 dB, C 3–4 dB and X 1–2 dB.
Limits: Dynamic range is not classification accuracy; a chronosequence is not a continuously observed single site.
Review depth: Publisher article extracts.

Technique: Compare pre and post fire HV scattering and fuel related information.
Reported finding: A 1.5 dB threshold achieved accuracy about 0.70 in the reported test.
Limits: Actual measurements are airborne; simulated mission conditions are not spaceborne NISAR validation.

sections.title: Reproducibility resources and reading boundaries
sections.body:
A public dataset associated with actual NISAR research
The Hayli Gubbi study has an author supplied Zenodo record containing NISAR SLC, Sentinel 1 and supporting materials. The record lists a NISAR SLC ZIP of about 1.3 GB and a complete deposit of about 2.3 GB. These are deposit sizes, not general NISAR product sizes. The archive provenance and published processing details should be checked together before replication.
Hayli Gubbi author dataset — Zenodo record 18500929
Official learning and mission science resources
The NISAR science publications index includes mission white papers across ecosystems, cryosphere and solid Earth. These describe requirements and intended measurements; they should not be counted as postlaunch experiments. The Cookbook supplies retrieval and array processing examples, with some historical proxy examples. The live User Guide defines product semantics and known issues.
NISAR publications and white papers
NISAR Data User Guide
NISAR Cookbook
MintPy release history and reader support
Search coverage and practical limits
The search combined official NASA/ISRO mission examples, publisher and DOI records, author datasets, relevant SAR literature and recent NISAR named studies. It expanded the prior review with soil moisture algorithm development, snow validation and error studies, regional L band time series, actual NISAR volcanic deformation and a large NISAR phase unwrapping preprint.
Unavailable primary full text is marked rather than replaced with an unchecked performance claim. Not every reported result was reimplemented. essentials.title: One spacecraft. Two radar instruments.
essentials.text: NISAR is a NASA–ISRO observatory launched on 30 July 2025. NASA supplies L-band radar (about 24 cm wavelength), and ISRO supplies S-band radar (about 9.4 cm). Both share a 12 m deployable reflector.

essentials.title: Earth observed through microwave echoes
essentials.text: The instrument sends microwave pulses and measures their echoes while flying roughly 747 km above Earth. Synthetic aperture processing combines echoes collected as the spacecraft moves. SweepSAR supports a broad swath of about 240 km, day and night and through ordinary cloud cover.

essentials.title: Return to the same geometry every 12 days
essentials.text: The satellite looks sideways to its left. Ascending and descending views differ and cannot simply be mixed. The 12-day repeat is for one geometry; clouds do not prevent acquisition, but snow, moisture, vegetation, terrain and atmosphere still influence measurements.

essentials.title: NASA data and ISRO data use different archives
essentials.text: All app inputs are L-band: NASA/ASF GCOV, GUNW, GOFF and SME2. Earthdata Login authorizes access; the configured collections and LSAR readers determine the band. S-band uses ISRO Bhoonidhi and is not supported here. Frequency A/B are subbands, not the L/S distinction.

essentials.title: A map footprint is not a guarantee of valid pixels
essentials.text: Discovery finds intersecting archive records. Processing must still check common coverage, channel, track, pass, mode, calibration and masks. Provisional data are only partly validated. The 2026 archive includes a permanent late-July to early-August gap.

essentials.title: Every result should answer: measured what, when and how?
essentials.text: Power is scattering strength; phase compares radar path; offsets compare recognizable image patterns; soil moisture is a modeled retrieval. The app retains exact files, array paths, dates, units, quality rules and parameters. Color alone is never the measurement.
